description: Solar capacity is calculated from the units you consume, not from a count of your appliances. How to work out the right system size for your Chennai home, with a worked example.

blocks.html: It is a natural assumption: add up the appliances, match the solar to them, done. But an appliance rating tells you how much power something draws while it is running, and solar sizing depends on something different — how many units your household actually consumes over a month. A one-tonne air conditioner running two hours a night and the identical unit running ten hours a night have the same rating and completely different energy footprints.

Start with units, not appliances

Your electricity bill states the units you consumed. That figure already accounts for how long everything runs, how often, and how efficient it is, which is why it is a far better starting point than any appliance list. Take a full year if you can. A Chennai household's consumption in April looks nothing like its consumption in December, and sizing to either extreme alone gives you the wrong answer.

blocks.text: How much a kilowatt generates here

blocks.html: As a planning figure, one kilowatt of well-installed, unshaded rooftop solar in Chennai produces roughly four to four and a half units a day averaged across the year. Some days are better, monsoon weeks are worse, and shading or dust pull the number down. So a 3 kW system lands somewhere in the region of 360 to 400 units a month, and a 5 kW system in the region of 600 to 675.

blocks.text: A worked example

blocks.html: Say your bills average 500 units a month across the year. At roughly 4 units per kW per day, you would need somewhere around 4 kW to generate a comparable quantity over a month. Then the practical constraints come in:
The final recommendation is where those constraints meet your consumption — which is why it rarely comes out as a round number pulled from an appliance count.

Tell your installer about what's coming, not just what's here. A new air conditioner, an electric vehicle, or a son or daughter moving back home can change consumption substantially. It is far cheaper to size for it at the start than to extend a system later.

blocks.text: Why oversizing is not the safe option

blocks.html: If a bigger system always paid for itself, sizing would be easy. It does not. Beyond the point where you are covering your own consumption, you are exporting surplus units, and export is generally worth less to you than the units you avoid buying. You also pay for panels, structure, and roof space you did not need. A system matched to your actual usage almost always gives a better return than one built to reach an impressive-sounding number.

blocks.text: Undersizing has its own cost

blocks.html: The opposite error is quietly common. A system too small for the household covers a modest slice of the bill, and the fixed costs of the project — structure, labour, wiring, commissioning — are spread across fewer units. The per-unit economics get worse, not better.

The honest answer is that this needs your bills and your roof in front of someone. Bring a year of statements to a free site inspection and we will work through the arithmetic with you. If your roof is on the smaller side, our guide to fitting solar onto a compact terrace covers what is realistic.

title: How to Compare Solar Quotes: Price, Brand, Warranty
description: Price, company, reviews, and warranty all matter when buying solar—but in what order? How to compare quotations properly and the red flags to watch for.

blocks.html: Price, company reputation, reviews, warranty — every one of them counts, and homeowners usually try to weigh all four at once. The difficulty is that two quotations for "5 kW rooftop solar" can describe genuinely different projects, so comparing the totals at the bottom of the page tells you almost nothing. The first job is to make the quotes comparable. Only then does the price difference mean something.

blocks.alt: ZeroEB team assembling a solar mounting structure on a Chennai rooftop

blocks.text: Start with scope, not price

blocks.html: Read each quotation for what it includes and, more revealingly, what it does not. Common items that appear in one quote and quietly vanish from another:
A quote that is fifteen percent cheaper because it excludes earthing and protection devices is not cheaper at all. You will pay for those items eventually, either in cash or in problems.

blocks.text: Then compare the specification

blocks.html: Ask every supplier for the same four numbers: total system wattage, number and wattage of panels, roof area required, and expected monthly generation for your address. Then look at the panel efficiency and temperature coefficient, the inverter type and rating, and the warranty terms for panels, inverter, and workmanship separately — they are usually different lengths, and the workmanship warranty is the one people forget to ask about.

blocks.text: Then judge the company

blocks.html: Your panels may carry a twenty-five year performance warranty, but a warranty is only worth as much as the ability to act on it. Reasonable things to check: how long they have been installing, whether you can visit or see photographs of completed local work, whether they offer maintenance after handover, and how they responded when you asked a difficult question during the site visit.

Reviews are useful, with one caveat — read the ones describing service two or three years after installation rather than the ones written the week the system was switched on. Anyone can be responsive during a sale.

Questions worth asking every supplier: Who performs the installation, your own team or a subcontractor? How are roof penetrations waterproofed? Is earthing included and will you show me the test readings? What is your response time for a service call in year three? What exactly is excluded from this price?

blocks.text: Red flags
Where price should sit

blocks.html: Once the quotes cover the same scope and comparable equipment, price becomes a fair basis for choosing. What rarely works out is treating the lowest number as the goal from the start. A rooftop plant is meant to run for two decades on a structure fixed to your roof; the saving from cutting corners on the parts you cannot see is small, and the cost of putting it right afterwards is not.

Our own approach is to quote the full scope in one place, which is why our installation service page lists both what is included and what is not. If you have quotations in hand and want a second opinion, send them across and we will talk you through the differences.

title: From an Empty Roof to a Working Solar Plant: Every Stage
description: What actually happens between signing off a solar quote and switching the system on—survey, design, structure, panels, inverter, wiring, testing, and commissioning.

blocks.html: An empty terrace is just unused space. A few days of planned work later, the same square footage is producing electricity every day for the next twenty years. Homeowners often ask what actually happens in between, how disruptive it is, and how long they should set aside. Here is the sequence we follow on a typical residential project.

blocks.alt: Solar mounting structure erected over an empty rooftop terrace in Chennai

blocks.text: 1. Site survey

blocks.html: Before anything is ordered, we measure the usable area, track shading through the day, check the structural condition of the roof, and look at your meter, distribution board, and cable routes. We go through a year of your electricity bills at the same time, because the roof decides what is possible and the bills decide what is worthwhile. This is covered in detail in our article on what a site inspection involves.

blocks.text: 2. System design

blocks.html: Next comes the layout: how many panels, in what rows, at what tilt and orientation, how they are grouped into strings, where the inverter is mounted, and how the cable runs. Getting this right on paper is what avoids improvisation on the roof — improvisation is where leaks and untidy wiring come from.

blocks.text: 3. Civil work and mounting structure

blocks.html: The structure goes up first. Depending on the roof, this means pedestals or foundations, drilling and anchoring, and waterproof sealing at every penetration. Then rails, clamps, alignment, and levelling. This is the stage where the terrace looks most like a construction site, and it is also the stage that most determines how the plant holds up over the years.

blocks.text: 4. Panel installation

blocks.html: Panels are lifted, positioned, aligned, and clamped to the manufacturer's specified torque, then connected into strings using MC4 connectors. This is the part everyone photographs, and it is genuinely satisfying to watch a bare frame fill in over a few hours.

blocks.text: 5. Inverter installation

blocks.html: The inverter is wall-mounted in a shaded, ventilated position with the clearances the manufacturer requires, then the DC and AC terminations are made and the unit is configured for your system.

blocks.text: 6. Electrical work and earthing

blocks.html: AC and DC wiring is routed and dressed, the earthing system is installed and connected, and isolators, MCBs, and protection devices are fitted. Cable management belongs to this stage too — every run secured, nothing chafing, everything labelled.

blocks.text: 7. Testing and commissioning

blocks.html: Before the system is handed over: voltage and polarity checks, insulation resistance measurement, earth continuity verification, inverter startup, and a performance check against expected output. Where the inverter supports it, monitoring is connected so you can see generation on your phone.

blocks.text: 8. Handover

blocks.html: We clear the site, walk you through the system, show you how to read your generation and what the inverter indicators mean, and hand over the documentation you will need for warranty claims and subsidy paperwork.

How long does it take? The installation itself for a typical residential system usually runs across a few working days once materials are on site. Around that sit lead times for equipment and the separate timelines for net metering and subsidy processing, which depend on the utility rather than on us.

blocks.text: What it means for your household

blocks.html: You do not need to vacate the house. There will be drilling noise during the structure work, roof access will be occupied for the duration, and there is normally a short planned power interruption when the connection is made at your distribution board. Beyond that, daily life carries on.
You can see finished projects across Chennai in our work gallery, or start with our solar installation in Chennai page if you want a full rooftop plant.

title: Small Terrace? How Much Solar You Can Actually Fit
description: A small roof does not rule out solar. How much area each kilowatt needs, how elevated structures free up space, and why a partial system is still worth installing.

blocks.html: Plenty of Chennai homes have a terrace that is already doing several jobs. There is a water tank in one corner, the staircase headroom in another, clothes lines across the middle, and a row of pots along the parapet. Owners look at what is left and conclude there is no room for solar. In most cases there is — just not as much as a larger roof would take, and that turns out to be fine.

blocks.alt: Elevated solar mounting structure over a compact Chennai terrace

blocks.text: The area each kilowatt needs

blocks.html: As a working figure, allow roughly 80 to 100 square feet of clear, unshaded area per kilowatt. Higher-efficiency panels sit at the lower end of that range, which is exactly when paying for them makes sense. In round terms:
These are planning numbers. The real figure depends on panel wattage, how the rows are laid out, and the walkway you need to leave for cleaning and maintenance.

blocks.text: The elevated structure changes the arithmetic

blocks.html: This is the single most useful option for a crowded terrace. Instead of occupying the floor, the array sits on a raised galvanised structure well above head height. The terrace underneath stays usable — clothes still dry there, plants still live there, and the space picks up welcome shade during summer. In effect the same square footage does two jobs.
It also lets the array span over obstructions that would otherwise break up the layout, and lifts the panels clear of shade cast by the parapet wall in the early morning and late afternoon.

blocks.text: Getting more out of a compact layout

blocks.html: Leave room to work. Panels need periodic cleaning and inspection. A layout that squeezes in one extra panel at the cost of any safe access will cost you more in awkward maintenance than the panel ever generates.

blocks.text: A smaller system is still a good system

blocks.html: The instinct is to feel that if you cannot wipe out the whole bill, it is not worth starting. In practice a 2 kW array on a compact roof still produces in the region of 240 to 270 units a month, and those are units you stop buying every single month for the next two decades. Solar does not have to be all or nothing to be worth doing.

What matters is sizing sensibly to what your roof and your consumption support, which is the same principle we cover in our guide to working out the right capacity. And if your usable space is on a sloped or sheet roof rather than a terrace, our article on installing without a flat terrace covers the options.
